extracted.intended_audience: graduate or advanced undergraduate students and researchers in algebraic topology
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook section explaining limits, lim^1, Ext and Hom calculations in (co)homology; transfer homomorphisms; constructions realizing polynomial mod-p cohomology rings; and local coefficients. Includes theorems, propositions, examples, and computational techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3F.8: exact sequence for union of subcomplexes
rubrics_metrics.description: For a CW complex X which is the union of an increasing sequence of subcomplexes X0 ⊂ X1 ⊂ ··· there is an exact sequence 0 → lim^1 hn−1(Xi) → hn(X) → lim hn(Xi) → 0 where h* is any reduced or unreduced cohomology theory. For any homology theory h* (reduced or unreduced) the natural maps lim→ hn(Xi) → hn(X) are isomorphisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the mapping telescope T of the inclusion sequence (T ≃ X) and a Mayer–Vietoris sequence for a decomposition T = T1 ∪ T2; the connecting maps are built from restriction maps and signs (ϕ vs δ). For reduced cohomology use the reduced telescope collapsing {x0}×[0,∞). For homology replace infinite products by direct sums in the corresponding diagram. Notes: Ker δ = 0 in the direct limit case and Coker δ = lim^1. The theorem gives the role of lim^1 as the obstruction between the cohomology of the union and the inverse limit of cohomologies of the pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example 3F.9: mapping telescope of degree p maps — anomalous cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: For the mapping telescope T of the sequence of degree p maps S^n → S^n → ··· (with Ti the union of the first i mapping cylinders), the inclusions induce the sequence ··· → Z -p→ Z → ··· on H^n(−; Z). From Theorem 3F.8 one deduces H^{n+1}(T; Z) ≅ Z_p/Z and H^k(T; Z) = 0 for k ≠ n+1, while homology gives H_n(T) ≅ Z[1/p].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates that cohomology of a union can behave very differently from the cohomologies of the pieces: each Ti has a Z in dimension n, but T has none in dimension n and instead a large uncountable group in dimension n+1. Contrast with homology where the pieces' H_n assemble to Z[1/p]. Use this as a caution when passing to limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example 3F.10: Moore space M(Z_{p^∞}, n) cohomology computation
rubrics_metrics.description: For X = M(Z_{p^∞}, n) expressed as the union of subspaces Xi, the reduced cohomology of Xi with Z coefficients consists of Z_{p^i} = Ext(Z_{p^i}, Z) in dimension n+1. The inclusion Xi ↪ Xi+1 induces inclusions on H_n and surjections on Ext, so the sequence ··· → H^{n+1}(X2; Z) → H^{n+1}(X1; Z) is that of Example 3F.6 and one deduces H^{n+1}(X; Z) ≅ Z_p and H^k(X; Z) = 0 for k ≠ n+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This example is related to mapping telescopes: view X as the mapping cone of inclusion S^n ↪ T; then long exact sequences for the pair reduce to the short exact sequences used earlier. Use universal coefficient theorem and free resolution diagrams to analyze induced maps on Ext.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computations of Ext for specific groups (Z_{p^∞}, Z[1/p])
rubrics_metrics.description: Ext(Z_{p^∞}, Z) ≅ Z_p and Ext(Z[1/p], Z) ≅ Z_p/Z. Explicit free resolutions are given: for Z_{p^∞} a resolution 0 → Z^∞ -ϕ→ Z^∞ → Z_{p^∞} → 0 with ϕ(px1 − x2, px2 − x3, ···), dualizing gives ϕ* whose cokernel identifies with Z_p. For Z[1/p] omit the first column / change sign to get ϕ(x1,x2,···) = (x1, x2 − p x1, x3 − p x2, ···) and ϕ* has image sums giving Z_p/Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an explicit linear-algebra-style description (infinite matrices) of the boundary maps and their duals; shows how p-adic integers and p-adic expansions appear from Coker ϕ* identifications. Useful model for concrete Ext computations in non-finitely generated cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3F.11: six-term exact sequences relating Hom and Ext
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an abelian group G and a short exact sequence 0 → A → B → C → 0, there are exact sequences 0 → Hom(G,A) → Hom(G,B) → Hom(G,C) → Ext(G,A) → Ext(G,B) → Ext(G,C) → 0 and 0 → Hom(C,G) → Hom(B,G) → Hom(A,G) → Ext(C,G) → Ext(B,G) → Ext(A,G) → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses a two-term free resolution of G and the long exact sequence of homology obtained from applying Hom(−,·) to a short exact sequence of chain complexes; dual construction yields the other sequence. Consequences: injections A ↪ B induce surjections Ext(B,C) → Ext(A,C); these exact sequences are practical tools for bootstrapping Ext/Hom computations and deducing (non)vanishing and surjectivity properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct-sum / direct-product Ext formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Two useful formulas: Ext(⊕_i A_i, B) ≅ ∏_i Ext(A_i, B) and Ext(A, ∏_i B_i) ≅ ∏_i Ext(A, B_i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these to reduce Ext computations for infinite direct sums or products to corresponding products of Ext groups. Examples in text: Ext(Q, Z) and Ext(Q/Z, Z) computations derived using decompositions into p-primary components and these formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3F.12: uncountability of Hom or Ext for non-finitely-generated groups
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is not finitely generated then either Hom(A, Z) or Ext(A, Z) is uncountable. Hence if H_n(X; Z) is not finitely generated then either H^n(X; Z) or H^{n+1}(X; Z) is uncountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: consider p-ranks and the map a ↦ p a; use facts that infinite direct sums of finite cyclic groups yield uncountable Ext, and that Ext(Z_{p^∞}, Z) ≅ Z_p is uncountable. Reduce to torsionfree or torsion cases and use exact sequences from Proposition 3F.11. Topological consequences: there is no space whose only nonvanishing H^n(X; Z) is a countable non-finitely-generated group like Q or Q/Z; H^1(X; Z) is always torsionfree. Use this proposition as an obstruction/result about realizability of cohomology groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer homomorphisms for finite-sheeted coverings (definition and basic properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an n-sheeted covering π: X̃ → X there is a chain-level transfer τ: C_k(X) → C_k(X̃) sending a singular simplex to the sum of its n lifts; it commutes with boundary and induces τ*: H^k(X; G) → H^k(X̃; G). Composition τ*π* equals multiplication by n, so ker π* consists of torsion elements of order dividing n (hence π* injective when coefficients are a field of characteristic 0 or prime not dividing n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: cohomology of X̃ must be larger than that of X except for torsion dividing n; for fields of suitable characteristic π* is injective and image can be characterized as invariant under the deck transformation group. Use transfer to compare cohomology of finite covers and quotients and to construct or control classes via averaging arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3G.1: image characterization using deck-group invariants
rubrics_metrics.description: Let π: X̃ → X be an n-sheeted covering defined by an action of a group Γ. For coefficients in a field F of characteristic 0 or a prime not dividing n, π*: H^k(X; F) → H^k(X̃; F) is injective with image equal to the Γ-invariant subgroup H^k(X̃; F)^Γ (classes fixed by all deck transformations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: use τ*π* = n and linear algebra over F to show injectivity and surjectivity onto invariants. Practical use: to identify the cohomology of quotient spaces as invariant subrings when the transfer averaging works (i.e., when dividing by n is valid in coefficients).

rubrics_metrics.name: Borel construction to convert group actions into free actions for cohomology computations
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a (possibly non-free) action of a finite group Γ on a space Y, the Borel construction Y ×_Γ EΓ (diagonal free action on Y × EΓ) produces a space whose cohomology is isomorphic to the Γ-invariant part of H^*(Y; coefficients) when the coefficient field has characteristic not dividing |Γ| and transfer arguments apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to realize quotient spaces with free covering actions homotopy equivalent to Borel constructions and to reduce cohomology computations for quotients to computing invariant subrings. Often used in conjunction with transfer (Proposition 3G.1) and finite group actions on spaces with known polynomial cohomology to produce new polynomial cohomology rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realizing polynomial mod-p cohomology rings via symmetric/permutation actions (CP^∞ product example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with Y = (CP^∞)^n with H^*(Y; Z_p) ≅ Z_p[y_1, ..., y_n] (|y_i| = 2). The symmetric group Σ_n acts by permuting factors; invariant polynomials form Z_p[σ_1, ..., σ_n] where σ_i are elementary symmetric polynomials (|σ_i| = 2i). If p does not divide |Σ_n| = n! (e.g., p > n) then by transfer/Borel construction the cohomology of the quotient realizes the polynomial ring Z_p[x_1, ..., x_n] with |x_i| = 2i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a basic method to produce polynomial cohomology rings with prescribed generator degrees; condition p ∤ |Γ| (so one can divide by |Γ| in coefficients) is crucial for the transfer/invariant identification to hold. Note: sometimes other constructions (e.g., Grassmannians) give the same rings without the p > n restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using Aut(Z_p) and Z_{p^∞} actions to realize single-variable polynomial rings and higher-degree generators
rubrics_metrics.description: Let π = Z_p and Γ = Aut(Z_p) (cyclic of order p−1) act on K(Z_p,1); induced action on H^*(K(Z_p,1); Z_p) shows the Γ-invariants form a polynomial algebra Z_p[x] with generator degrees related to p−1 (e.g., |x| = 2p−2). Replacing Z_p by Z_{p^∞} and using the split surjection Aut(Z_{p^∞}) → Aut(Z_p) yields spaces BZ_{p^∞} whose Z_p cohomology is Z_p[β] with |β| = 2, and Borel constructions produce polynomial rings Z_p[y] with |y| any even divisor of 2(p−1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key steps: compute action on H^1 and H^2 via multiplication by m in Aut; deduce invariants (only certain powers survive), and use Borel construction and splitting of automorphism restriction maps. Useful to obtain single-variable polynomial algebras with generator degrees beyond 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product constructions with permutation and factorwise automorphism actions (Examples 3G.6–3G.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form X = (BZ_{p^∞})^n and let Γ be generated by permutations of factors combined with factorwise Zd-actions (Zd a subgroup of Aut(Z_p) of order d). For suitable congruence conditions on p (e.g., p ≡ 1 mod d) and p > n to avoid divisibility issues, the invariant subring H^*(X; Z_p)^Γ is a polynomial ring Z_p[y_{2d}, y_{4d}, ..., y_{2nd}] (or variants with q replacing last degree) realizing a wide family of degree sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction yields many realizable multivariable polynomial cohomology rings; conditions on p (congruences, p > n) ensure Γ embeds appropriately and transfer works. Variations (e.g., choosing subgroup with product-of-entries constraint) change the last generator degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification sketch: realizability of polynomial algebras Z_p[y_1,...,y_n]
rubrics_metrics.description: For odd primes p, every realizable polynomial algebra Z_p[y_1, ..., y_n] arises as an invariant ring Z_p[β_1, ..., β_n]^Γ for some finite group Γ acting on the polynomial algebra in degree-2 classes. Basic realizable examples come from classifying spaces of Lie groups (S^1, SU(n), Sp(n), SO(2k), G2, F4, E6, E7, E8) with specified degree sequences and prime restrictions, together with two infinite families and 30 sporadic exceptions (tables provided). The order of Γ often equals the product of the degrees, and congruence conditions on p (e.g., p ≡ 1 mod d) arise to embed Γ into Aut(Z_p^n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a summary of deep results (Dwyer–Miller–Wilkerson and others) describing which degree sequences are realizable; for many entries the transfer/Borel construction method suffices when p does not divide |Γ|, while other constructions are needed when congruence conditions fail. The text points to Kane and Notbohm for further study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local coefficients via modules (definition and chain-level construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a path-connected space X with universal cover �5Ctilde{X} and fundamental group π, the singular chain groups C_n(�5Ctilde{X}) are left Z[π]-modules. For a left Z[π]-module M define C_n(X; M) = C_n(�5Ctilde{X}) ⊗_{Z[π]} M and C^n(X; M) = Hom_{Z[π]}(C_n(�5Ctilde{X}), M). Their homology/cohomology are the (co)homology groups with local coefficients in M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful handling of left/right module structures is required (a left module can be regarded as a right module via γ acting by γ^{-1}). Tensoring over Z[π] factors out the π-action. This construction generalizes ordinary (co)homology to non-simply-connected spaces and underlies phenomena such as Poincar�E9 duality with twisted coefficients.
